meta.title: Who really said "Life is a series of natural and spontaneous changes. Don't resist them; that only creates sorrow. Let reality be reality"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Lao Tzu. This line was written by self-help author Vernon Howard in 1967 as his own paraphrase of Taoism, then misattributed to Lao Tzu in 1985.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Life is a series of natural and spontaneous changes. Don't resist them; that only creates sorrow. Let reality be reality'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lao Tzu. Vernon Howard wrote it in 1967 as his own explanation of Taoism; it’s not in the Tao Te Ching. Here’s the paper trail.

answer.label: Not Lao Tzu — written by Vernon Howard
answer.sourceLine: The exact wording comes from Vernon Howard’s 1967 self-help book The Mystic Path to Cosmic Power (p. 112), where Howard offered it as his own plain-English explanation of Taoist thought — not as a translation of Lao Tzu. It appears nowhere in the Tao Te Ching. The line was later shortened and pinned on Lao Tzu by Susan Hayward’s 1985 A Guide for the Advanced Soul, and spread from there across books and the Internet.

source.excerpt: Life is a series of natural and spontaneous changes. Don’t resist them; don’t wish things were different. That only creates sorrow. Go along. Let reality be reality. Let things flow naturally forward in whatever way they like. Be like a pebble carried effortlessly along the stream of life.
trail: Stefan Stenudd (Taoistic.com) traces the wording to Vernon Howard’s The Mystic Path to Cosmic Power (1967), where Howard is explaining Taoism in his own words, not quoting Lao Tzu.
Wikiquote places the line in its Misattributed section, noting the origin is unknown and it is not found in the Dao De Jing.
The name “Lao Tzu” was attached later via Susan Hayward’s 1985 anthology A Guide for the Advanced Soul, from which it spread across quote sites and social media.
source.excerptNote: Vernon Howard’s original 1967 passage — his own explanation of Taoism. The popular “Lao Tzu” version trims it to the smoother middle lines.

author.name: Vernon Howard
author.heading: Vernon Howard
author.bio: Vernon Linwood Howard (1918–1992) was an American author and lecturer on self-awareness and inner life who began writing in the late 1950s and founded the New Life Foundation in 1979. He wrote dozens of popular books drawing loosely on mysticism and Eastern thought; his readership has been estimated in the millions. In The Mystic Path to Cosmic Power he paraphrased Taoist ideas in his own words — one of those passages, not a genuine Lao Tzu text, became the “Lao Tzu” quote seen everywhere today.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is one of the Internet’s most-shared “Lao Tzu” quotes — and it isn’t his. The wording is modern, written by a 20th-century self-help author.

items.why: Pinned on the ancient Taoist sage across Goodreads, BrainyQuote, and social media, but it appears nowhere in the Tao Te Ching. Wikiquote lists it as Misattributed, noting its origin is not found in the Dao De Jing.
The line is Howard’s own explanation of Taoism in The Mystic Path to Cosmic Power (p. 112); Stefan Stenudd shows Howard was explaining, not quoting.
A shortened form first appears credited to Lao Tzu in Hayward’s anthology A Guide for the Advanced Soul, and spread through later books and the web from there.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought echoes Taoism, but the words are Vernon Howard’s — a 1967 paraphrase, not a Lao Tzu text.

context.heading: How a self-help paraphrase became ‘ancient wisdom’
lead: The passage reads like Taoism — go with the flow, don’t resist change, let reality be reality — which is exactly why it stuck to Lao Tzu so easily. But it was written in plain 1960s American English by Vernon Howard, a prolific self-help author, as his own gloss on Taoist thinking. Howard never claimed to be quoting anyone; he was explaining a philosophy in his own voice.

The jump to “—Lao Tzu” came through a quotation anthology. Susan Hayward’s 1985 A Guide for the Advanced Soul printed a trimmed version with Lao Tzu’s name attached, and from there it multiplied across later books, greeting cards, and social media — a textbook case of an author’s paraphrase hardening into a fake ancient quotation.
context.detailsSummary: The wording swap between Howard and the ‘Lao Tzu’ version
detailsBody: Howard’s original (1967) is longer and folksier: it adds “don’t wish things were different,” “Go along,” and closes with “Be like a pebble carried effortlessly along the stream of life.”
The popular “Lao Tzu” version drops those lines, keeping the smoother core — the shortening that first appears attributed to Lao Tzu in Hayward’s 1985 anthology.
context.pull: Howard wasn’t quoting Lao Tzu — he was explaining Taoism in his own words.
